title: Shrines
translation: The way the Ise priestess lives at the Shrine in the Fields while she prepares for Ise struck me as about as graceful and lovely as anything gets. Buddhist words are off limits there, so they use homemade Japanese ones instead: the Buddha is "the middle one", and scripture is "dyed paper". I like that.

Shrines in general have a quiet grace you can't let go of. The old woods around them already feel different, and then there's the sacred fence all the way around, and the white cloth strips hanging from the sacred evergreen branches. How could that not be wonderful?
My favourites: Ise, Kamo, Kasuga, Hirano, Sumiyoshi, Miwa, Kibune, Yoshida, Ōharano, Matsunoo, and Umenomiya.

literal: The state of the Ise Priestess residing at the Nonomiya: that, I felt, was the very height of graceful and delightful things.
That they avoid (words like) sutra and Buddha, and say 'nakago' and 'dyed paper' and the like, is also delightful.
In general, shrines of the gods are things hard to give up, and graceful.
The scenery of the aged forests is already out of the ordinary, and with sacred fences all around and bark-cloth hung on the sakaki: how could that not be splendid?
Especially delightful are Ise, Kamo, Kasuga, Hirano, Sumiyoshi, Miwa, Kibune, Yoshida, Ōharano, Matsunoo and Umenomiya.

notes.text: The {斎宮|さいくう} was an unmarried imperial princess chosen to serve the gods at the Ise Shrine. Before going to Ise she spent about a year purifying herself at the Nonomiya, the 'Shrine in the Fields', in Sagano west of the capital. Readers would remember the Sakaki chapter of the Tale of Genji, which opens there.

Around the Ise priestess, Buddhist words were taboo ({忌|い}み{詞|ことば}), because Buddhism belonged to death and funerals, the worst pollution for the gods. The taboo words are Chinese loans (仏 butsu, 経 kyō), and the replacements are native Japanese: the Buddha is 'the middle one' ({中子|なかご}), scripture is 'dyed paper' ({染紙|そめがみ}), from the coloured paper sutras were written on. The official list in the Engishiki (927) goes on: a temple is 'tile-roof' (temples had tiled roofs, houses did not), a pagoda is 'araragi', a monk is 'long-hair' (monks shaved their heads). Imagine English church words, which mostly come from Latin and Greek, replaced by plain old English: 'holy writ' for scripture, 'monk-house' for monastery. A Buddhist priest enjoying all this is part of the charm.
{榊|さかき}: an evergreen tree sacred in Shinto. {木綿|ゆふ}: strips of white bark-fibre cloth hung on it as offerings. Not cotton, despite the kanji.

Kenkō's family, the Urabe, are traditionally said to have been priests of the Yoshida Shrine, which is where the name 'Yoshida Kenkō' comes from, though recent research doubts the connection. All eleven shrines in the list are among the Twenty-Two Shrines that received special imperial support, but Kenkō writes it like a list of favourite places.
